# Gateway 1 – Building Safety Act 2022 Regime

## What Stage It Applies

**Gateway 1 applies at the planning application stage.** It is the first of three "gateways" in the building safety regime for higher-risk buildings, and it operates within the planning system (as opposed to Gateways 2 and 3, which operate within the building control system under the Building Safety Regulator).

## What Gateway 1 Requires

For relevant high-rise residential developments, Gateway 1 requires that **fire safety matters are considered at the earliest design stage**, embedding fire safety into the planning process. In practice, the applicant must submit a **Fire Statement** with the planning application.

The Fire Statement addresses site- and building-level fire safety considerations relevant to the planning process, such as:

- Access and facilities for the fire and rescue service (e.g. appliance access, water supplies for firefighting)
- Site layout in relation to fire safety
- The principle of the development in fire safety terms
- Other matters within the scope of the local planning authority's remit

The intention is to ensure fire safety is not left to later stages but is designed in from the outset.

## Who Is the Statutory Consultee

**The Health and Safety Executive (HSE)** is the statutory consultee for Gateway 1.

The local planning authority must consult the HSE on relevant planning applications, and the HSE provides advice on the fire safety aspects of the proposed development. This was introduced via amendments to the **Town and Country Planning (Development Management Procedure) (England) Order 2015** and came into force on **1 August 2021**.

## Application to Your Scheme

The proposed development — **a 9-storey (32m tall) residential block** — meets the height threshold for a "higher-risk building" (**at least 18m in height, or at least 7 storeys, containing at least two residential units**). It therefore falls within the regime, and Gateway 1 requirements will apply to the planning application.

# Safety Case Report Requirements under the Building Safety Act 2022

## Context: Higher-Risk Building

A 22-storey residential tower qualifies as a **higher-risk building** under the Act. The threshold is a building that is **at least 18 metres in height OR at least 7 storeys**, containing **at least 2 residential units**. This building comfortably exceeds those criteria, so the full higher-risk regime applies, regulated by the **Building Safety Regulator (BSR)** (part of the Health and Safety Executive).

## The Safety Case Report Requirement

The **Principal Accountable Person (PAP)** must produce a **Safety Case Report** which:

- **Identifies** the building safety risks (defined as risks of spread of fire and/or structural failure)
- **Assesses** those risks
- Demonstrates that **reasonable steps** are being taken to **prevent** a building safety risk materialising and to **reduce the seriousness** of an incident if one does occur
- Draws on the underlying **safety case** (the body of evidence, assessments and management arrangements)

The report must be **kept under review** and revised as necessary — it is a living document, not a one-off exercise.

## When It Must Be Produced

- The PAP must prepare the Safety Case Report **as soon as reasonably practicable** after the building is registered.
- **Registration** with the BSR became **mandatory** — occupied higher-risk buildings had to be registered during the transition window (the requirement came into force with the regulator able to require registration from **April 2023**, with occupied buildings needing to be registered by **1 October 2023**).
- It is a **criminal offence to allow a higher-risk building to be occupied if it is not registered.**
- The report itself is produced when required and **must be submitted to the BSR on request** (the BSR calls in reports on a prioritised basis).

## Key Ongoing Duties (Part 4 obligations)

The PAP must also:
- Apply for a **Building Assessment Certificate** when directed by the BSR (must be displayed in the building)
- Establish a **mandatory occurrence reporting** system
- Prepare a **Residents' Engagement Strategy** and provide safety information to residents
- Maintain the **golden thread** of information

## Penalties for Failure to Register or Comply

| Offence | Penalty |
|---------|---------|
| **Failing to register** an occupied higher-risk building | Criminal offence; on conviction — **imprisonment up to 2 years and/or an unlimited fine** |
| **Failing to comply with a compliance notice** issued by the BSR | Criminal offence — **imprisonment up to 2 years and/or an unlimited fine** |
| **Contravening Part 4 duties** (e.g. safety case, assessment, resident engagement) | Enforcement action, compliance/improvement notices; continued non-compliance can lead to **prosecution** |

The BSR can also issue **compliance notices** and **improvement notices**, and ultimately pursue prosecution. Offences can be committed by the organisation and by individuals where there is consent, connivance or neglect.

# Principal Designer Competence Under the HRB Dutyholder Regime

## Context

Under the **Building Safety Act 2022** and the **Building Regulations etc. (Amendment) (England) Regulations 2023**, the dutyholder regime for building regulations compliance came into force on **1 October 2023**. This is distinct from (though overlapping with) the CDM 2015 Principal Designer role. For Higher-Risk Buildings (HRBs — generally 18m+ or 7+ storeys with residential/hospital/care uses), the Building Safety Regulator (BSR) oversight applies.

## Competence Required

The Principal Designer (a building regs dutyholder) must demonstrate competence covering:

- **Skills, knowledge, experience and behaviours (SKEB)** — the statutory formulation of competence
- **Relevant capability** to plan, manage and monitor the design work so that, if built, it would comply with all relevant building regulations
- Ability to **coordinate design work of others** to ensure compliance
- Understanding of how their design decisions affect building regulations compliance, including fire safety and structural integrity for HRBs
- Organisational capability (if a firm) — sufficient systems, resources and processes, not just individual competence

The client has a **duty to check and be satisfied** the appointee has this competence *before* appointment.

## The Underpinning Standard

- **PAS 8671:2022** — *Built environment. Framework for competence of individual Principal Designers.* This defines the SKEB benchmark for individuals acting as PD.
- **PAS 8672:2022** — equivalent framework for the **Principal Contractor**.
- **PAS 8670:2022** — the overarching built environment competence framework (baseline for building safety).
- **BS 8670-1:2024** — the core criteria for building safety competence frameworks (sits above the PAS documents).

For architects specifically, the **ARB** and **RIBA** have developed competence frameworks and mandatory CPD (including fire safety/building safety) aligned to these standards. Note: being ARB-registered does **not automatically** make an architect a competent PD — the PAS 8671 SKEB must be separately evidenced for each project's complexity.

## Personal Liability Risk

The risks are significant and increasingly personal:

| Risk area | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| **Criminal liability** | Breaches of building regulations dutyholder obligations are criminal offences. Individuals can be prosecuted, not just companies. |
| **Penalties** | Unlimited fines and, for serious offences, **up to 2 years' imprisonment**. |
| **Extended limitation** | The BSA extended the limitation period under the Defective Premises Act 1972 to **15 years prospectively and 30 years retrospectively** for certain claims. |
| **Overlapping CDM liability** | Separate criminal exposure under CDM 2015 as a PD for health and safety. |
| **Professional consequences** | ARB/RIBA disciplinary action; loss of registration; reputational damage. |
| **Insurance** | PII may not respond to criminal penalties; check policy wording carefully — building safety exclusions are increasingly common. |

## Practical Cautions

1. **Do not accept the appointment beyond your competence** — you must decline if you lack the SKEB for the project's complexity.
2. **Document your competence assessment** and the client's verification.
3. **Distinguish the two PD roles** — the building regs PD (BSA) and the CDM PD (health & safety) are legally separate, though often held by the same party.
4. **Maintain evidence trails** for design decisions and compliance monitoring, especially the **golden thread** of information for HRBs.

# Transitional Provisions for In-Flight HRB Projects

## Background

When the Building Safety Act 2022 regime came into force, the **Higher-Risk Buildings (Transitional Provisions) (England) Regulations 2023** were introduced to manage the shift of higher-risk building (HRB) work from local authority/approved inspector control to the **Building Safety Regulator (BSR)** as the sole building control authority for HRBs.

## The Cut-Off Date

**1 October 2023** is the key date. This is when the new HRB regime under the Building Safety Act took effect and the BSR became the building control authority for higher-risk building work.

## Conditions to Remain "In-Flight" (Stay Under Old Regime)

A project can continue under the **old building control regime** (avoiding transition to BSR) if, **before 1 October 2023**, both of the following were satisfied:

1. **An initial notice** was given, OR **a building notice / full plans** were deposited with the local authority; **AND**
2. **Work had "sufficiently progressed"** — this generally means work had **started** on the relevant building work.

The definition of "sufficiently progressed" is important:
- For **new buildings**: work has started where the pouring of concrete for either the permanent placement of trench, pad or raft foundations, or the permanent placement of piling has begun.
- For **other work** (e.g., to existing buildings): work has started where that work has begun.

## What Triggers a Forced Transition to BSR

Even if a project qualified as in-flight, transition to BSR oversight is **forced** in these circumstances:

1. **Work was not sufficiently progressed by the deadline** — the transitional window generally required work to have started by **6 April 2024** (the transitional period ran for six months from 1 October 2023). If work had not sufficiently progressed by **6 April 2024**, the project **must transition** to the new BSR regime.

2. **Lapse of the initial notice / approval** — if the initial notice ceases to have effect, or the deposited plans lapse, the protection falls away and BSR oversight applies.

3. **Cancellation of the initial notice** by the approved inspector or local authority.

## Practical Summary for the Contractor

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| Cut-off date | **1 October 2023** (regime start); work must have started by **6 April 2024** |
| Can they stay under old regime? | Yes — if a valid notice was deposited **before 1 October 2023** AND work was **sufficiently progressed** (started) by **6 April 2024** |
| Forced transition triggers | Work not sufficiently progressed by 6 April 2024; lapse or cancellation of the initial notice; deposited plans lapsing |

## Recommendation

The contractor should:
- Confirm the **date of deposit** of the initial notice/full plans.
- Evidence that **work genuinely started** (documented foundation/piling records dated before 6 April 2024).
- If work did **not** start in time, they **must** submit a **building control approval application** to the **BSR** and comply with the Gateway regime.

> **Caveat:** These regulations are detailed and fact-specific. Given the compliance and liability implications, the contractor should obtain confirmation from a building control professional or legal adviser on the exact status of their specific project.

# Golden Thread Information Requirements for HRBs

This relates to the **Building Safety Act 2022** and specifically the **Higher-Risk Buildings (Golden Thread Information) Regulations 2024** (in England). Here's a breakdown of the three areas your client is asking about.

## 1. What Information Must Be Maintained

The golden thread must contain the information needed to demonstrate that the building is safe and that safety is being managed. There isn't an exhaustive fixed list, but it should include:

- **Design and construction information** – drawings, specifications, plans, and details of design intent
- **Fire safety information** – fire strategy, compartmentation, means of escape, fire-fighting provisions
- **Structural safety information** – structural design and calculations relevant to building safety
- **Change control records** – documentation of design and construction changes
- **The Building Regulations compliance information** – demonstrating how compliance was achieved
- **Details of the building's systems** – e.g. ventilation, smoke control, evacuation systems
- **Information relevant to managing building safety risks** in occupation

The key legal test is that it captures information **relevant to the building safety risks** (spread of fire and structural failure).

## 2. What Format

The regulations set out specific format principles. The golden thread information must be:

- **Stored digitally / electronically** (not paper-based as the primary format)
- **Kept securely** – with appropriate protection against unauthorised access, loss, or damage
- **A single source of truth** – accurate, consistent, and up to date
- **Accessible and retrievable** – available to those who need it, in a format they can use
- **Presented in a way that can be understood** by relevant persons
- **Maintained** so that historic versions/changes can be tracked (version control)

The intent is a live, managed information system — not a static document dump.

## 3. When Handover Obligations Are Triggered

The golden thread has different duty-holders across the building lifecycle:

**During design and construction (Building Regulations regime):**
- The **client, principal designer, and principal contractor** are responsible for creating and maintaining the golden thread.

**At the transition to occupation:**
- The golden thread must be **handed over to the Principal Accountable Person (PAP)** so it is in place **before the building is occupied**.
- This handover is tied to the **completion certificate / building control approval** stage and the point at which the building becomes occupied.
- The information must be transferred in a state that allows the PAP/AP to continue maintaining it and to fulfil their in-occupation duties.

**During occupation:**
- The **Accountable Person(s)/PAP** must keep the golden thread up to date and maintain it for the life of the building.

## Practical Recommendation

I'd suggest your client:
1. Establish **information standards and protocols early** (aligned with BS 8644 / ISO 19650 principles).
2. Clarify **contractually** who is responsible for each element and for the handover.
3. Ensure the **digital system chosen supports the format requirements** and can be transferred cleanly to the PAP.

Before answering, note that the CSRD landscape shifted significantly in 2025. The EU's **Omnibus package** (proposed February 2025) and the **"Stop the Clock" Directive** (adopted April 2025) have:

- **Delayed reporting** by two years for the "wave 2" and "wave 3" companies not yet reporting
- Proposed **raising thresholds substantially** (e.g., to 1,000+ employees), which if adopted would take many mid-sized companies out of scope entirely

The analysis below covers both the **original rules** and the **likely revised position** — you need to track this closely as it's still moving.

## 1. Is the group in scope?

There are two separate questions here:

### (a) Do the German subsidiaries qualify individually?
Under the original CSRD, an EU company is in scope if it exceeds 2 of 3 thresholds:
- Balance sheet: €25m
- Net turnover: €50m
- 250 employees

Each subsidiary has ~300 employees and (presumably) significant turnover, so **each likely qualifies as a "large undertaking"** individually — subject to the balance sheet test and confirming they aren't exempted.

**Subsidiary exemption:** A subsidiary can be exempted if it is included in the **consolidated sustainability report of its parent**. But the UK parent is a **third-country parent** — its report must be prepared under ESRS or an equivalent standard for the exemption to apply. If the UK parent doesn't report to that standard, the German subsidiaries cannot rely on the exemption and must report individually.

### (b) The third-country (non-EU parent) rule
CSRD has a specific regime for **non-EU groups**. The UK group falls in scope if:
- EU-generated **net turnover > €150m** (you have €180m — **exceeded**), AND
- It has either a **large/listed EU subsidiary**, or an **EU branch** with turnover > €40m

With €180m EU turnover and two large German subsidiaries, the **third-country reporting obligation is triggered**.

|-------|------------------|------------------|----------------------|
| German subs as large non-listed undertakings | FY2025 | 2026 | **Delayed to FY2027** (published 2028) |
| Third-country parent consolidated report | FY2028 | 2029 | Under review |

Your subsidiaries fall into the **"wave 3" category (large non-listed EU undertakings)** — originally FY2025, **now delayed to FY2027** under Stop the Clock (assuming thresholds unchanged).

## 3. Assurance requirement

- Starts at **limited assurance** (not reasonable assurance).
- The Commission may move to reasonable assurance later, but this has been **deprioritised/removed** in the Omnibus direction.
- Assurance can be provided by the statutory auditor or, where a Member State permits, an independent assurance services provider. **Germany** has indicated auditors will perform this.

## Recommended actions

They insert new provisions into the Companies Act 2006 (notably ss.414CA and 414CB) and the associated disclosure requirements.

## Does It Apply to Your Company?

**Yes – almost certainly.**

For a **large private company** (i.e. not a traded company/banking/insurance company subject to different tests), the regime applies where the company meets **both** of these thresholds in the relevant financial year:

1. **More than 500 employees**; **and**
2. **Turnover of more than £500m.**

Your company:
- **600 employees** → exceeds 500 ✓
- **£700m turnover** → exceeds £500m ✓

Both thresholds are met, so the disclosure obligation applies. (Note: the £500m turnover threshold is specific to this climate regime and is distinct from the ordinary Companies Act "large company" size thresholds.)

One point worth checking: if this company is part of a group, the tests are applied to the individual company's own figures for these purposes, and separate parent/subsidiary considerations may arise.

## What Must Be Disclosed

Under **s.414CB CA 2006**, the disclosures broadly track the **TCFD (Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures)** four-pillar structure. The company must disclose:

**1. Governance**
- A description of the governance arrangements in relation to assessing and managing climate-related risks and opportunities.

**2. Strategy / Risk & Opportunity Identification**
- The principal climate-related risks and opportunities arising in connection with the company's operations, and the time periods over which they are assessed.
- A description of how these are identified, assessed and managed.

**3. Risk Management Integration**
- How processes for identifying, assessing and managing climate-related risks are integrated into the company's overall risk management process.

**4. Metrics, Targets and Resilience**
- Analysis of the **resilience** of the business model and strategy, taking into account different climate-related scenarios.
- The **targets** used to manage climate-related risks/opportunities and performance against them.
- The **key performance indicators (KPIs)** used to assess progress, and the calculation methodology.

**"Comply or explain" element:** Where the company has not undertaken certain analysis (e.g. scenario analysis or set targets/KPIs), it must **explain why** it considers that disclosure is not necessary/appropriate. Note this "explain" flexibility applies to a *limited* set of items – governance and risk-description elements are essentially mandatory.

## Where It Must Be Disclosed

- The disclosures must be included in the **Strategic Report** (as part of the annual report and accounts).
- Specifically, under **s.414CA**, they form a distinct part of the non-financial and sustainability information within the strategic report.
- They must therefore be **filed and made public** in the ordinary way alongside the annual accounts.

## Practical Points for the CFO

- **Data and process lead time:** Scenario analysis and KPI methodology can take significant time to develop – start early.
- **Director responsibility:** The strategic report is a director-approved document; directors are responsible for the adequacy of these disclosures.
- **Interaction with future reporting:** This regime sits alongside SECR (Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting) obligations, which likely already apply – ensure consistency between the two.

Under the **Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES)**, set out in the *Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property) (England and Wales) Regulations 2015*:

- The current minimum standard is **EPC Band E** (an asset rating of at least E).

| Renting sub-standard property for **3 months or more** | Up to **20% of rateable value**, minimum £10,000, **maximum £150,000** |
| Providing false/misleading information on the PRS Exemptions Register | Up to **£5,000** |

# MEES Exemption for Non-Domestic Property

## Which Exemption Applies

Based on the facts you've described, the relevant exemption is the **"seven-year payback" exemption** (sometimes called the "all relevant energy efficiency improvements have been made" exemption route, but specifically here the seven-year payback test).

Under MEES regulations for non-domestic property, a landlord is not required to install a measure where the expected value of savings on energy bills over a **7-year period** is less than the cost of installing that measure. If no qualifying improvement meets the seven-year payback test, the property is effectively exempt from having to reach Band E.

## How Long It Lasts

The exemption lasts for **5 years**.

After the 5-year period expires, the exemption ends and the landlord must try again to improve the property (or register a new exemption if one still applies).

## Evidence Required for the PRS Exemptions Register

To register the seven-year payback exemption, you must upload/provide:

1. **A copy of the report** (or relevant sections) prepared by a qualified person demonstrating the payback calculation, OR the three quotations approach:
   - **Three separate quotations** from qualified installers for purchasing and installing the recommended measure, each confirming the cost, AND
   - Written confirmation/evidence that you are satisfied the installation of the measure would not pay for itself through energy savings within seven years.

2. **The relevant measure(s)** in question — details of the recommended energy efficiency improvement(s) being relied upon.

3. Standard registration details:
   - **The address** of the property
   - **A copy of the valid EPC** for the property (showing it is below Band E)

## Key Points to Note

- The seven-year payback is calculated using a prescribed methodology comparing installation cost against the value of expected energy savings over seven years.
- Exemptions are **not transferable** — a new owner/landlord must register their own exemption (though they benefit from a temporary 6-month exemption on becoming the landlord).
- The exemption must be **self-certified and registered before** you continue to let, or continue letting, the sub-standard property.

# Scottish EPC Regime for Non-Domestic Property

## How Scotland Differs from England & Wales

Scotland operates a **distinct EPC and energy efficiency regime** because building standards and energy efficiency are devolved matters. Key differences include:

**Legislative framework:**
- Scotland: EPCs governed under the *Energy Performance of Buildings (Scotland) Regulations 2008*, with the key non-domestic mechanism being the *Assessment of Energy Performance of Non-domestic Buildings (Scotland) Regulations 2016* ("the Section 63 regime").
- England & Wales: EPCs under the *Energy Performance of Buildings (England and Wales) Regulations 2012*, with MEES under the *Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property) (England and Wales) Regulations 2015*.

**EPC display:**
- In Scotland, there is a specific requirement to **affix the EPC** to the building (e.g., in a plant room/boiler room) for certain non-domestic buildings, and to display it.

**Assessment methodology:**
- Both use SBEM-based calculations, but the compliance obligations attached differ significantly.

---

## Section 63 Action Plan Trigger

The **Section 63** regime (named after s.63 of the *Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009*) is Scotland's distinctive mechanism.

**Trigger conditions — an Action Plan is required when:**
1. The building is **non-domestic**, and
2. It has a floor area **greater than 1,000 m²**, and
3. There is a **sale** of the building or the **grant of a new lease** (to a new tenant).

**Exemptions include:**
- Buildings already meeting 2002 building standards (or later) energy requirements
- Certain building types (e.g., places of worship, listed buildings in some circumstances, buildings due for demolition, etc.)

**What the Action Plan requires:**
- On a triggering event, the owner must commission an assessment producing:
  - An **EPC**, and
  - An **Action Plan** identifying targeted improvement measures.
- The owner then either:
  - **Carries out the improvement works** within a set period (typically 3.5 years / 42 months), **OR**
  - **Reports/defers** by measuring and reporting operational energy ratings ("Display Energy Certificate" style operational reporting) annually instead.

The Action Plan and (where relevant) improvement/reporting documents are lodged on the **Scottish EPC Register**.

---

## Does MEES Apply in Scotland?

**No.** The **Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES)** regime — which prohibits letting sub-standard (below EPC E) property in England & Wales — **does not apply in Scotland**.

- There is **no equivalent EPC minimum rating threshold** below which a landlord is prohibited from letting non-domestic property in Scotland.
- Scotland's parallel policy lever is the **Section 63 Action Plan** approach described above, which focuses on *improvement measures/operational reporting* rather than an outright *letting/sale prohibition* based on a minimum band.

*(Note: For the domestic private rented sector, Scotland has developed separate proposals over time, but these are distinct from the non-domestic Section 63 regime and from E&W MEES.)*

---

## Practical Summary for the Landlord

| Issue | Scotland | England & Wales |
|-------|----------|-----------------|
| EPC required on sale/let | Yes | Yes |
| Minimum EPC letting threshold (MEES) | **No** | Yes (currently E) |
| Action Plan on sale/new lease | **Yes, if >1,000 m²** | No |
| Improvement obligation | Via Section 63 Action Plan | Via MEES compliance |

**Recommended next steps:** Confirm the property's floor area (the 1,000 m² threshold is decisive), check whether any Section 63 exemption applies, and instruct a qualified assessor to produce the EPC and, if triggered, the Action Plan before marketing/completing the transaction.

# UK F-Gas Regulation: GWP Restrictions for New Stationary Equipment

## Important Context on Your Specific Application

An 800kW air-cooled chiller falls under **stationary air-conditioning/refrigeration equipment**, but it's worth being precise about which bans actually apply, because there's a common misconception here.

## What Bans Actually Exist Under Retained EU 517/2014

The UK retained the EU F-Gas Regulation post-Brexit, and the key placing-on-the-market prohibitions for stationary equipment are:

| Equipment type | GWP threshold | Effective date |
|---|---|---|
| Domestic refrigerators/freezers | GWP ≥ 150 | Jan 2015 |
| Commercial refrigerators/freezers (hermetically sealed) | GWP ≥ 2500 | Jan 2020 |
| Commercial refrigerators/freezers (hermetically sealed) | GWP ≥ 150 | Jan 2022 |
| Stationary refrigeration equipment | GWP ≥ 2500 | Jan 2020 |
| Multipack centralised commercial refrigeration (≥40kW) | GWP ≥ 150 | Jan 2022 |
| **Movable room AC (self-contained)** | GWP ≥ 150 | Jan 2020 |
| **Split AC systems <3kg charge** | GWP ≥ 750 | Jan 2025 |

## Critical Point for Your Chiller

**There is no specific outright GWP ban on large air-cooled chillers of this size** under the current retained regulation. The GWP ≥ 2500 stationary refrigeration ban has an explicit exemption for equipment intended for applications **below −50°C**, and chillers are generally regulated indirectly rather than by a dedicated product ban.

The real constraint is the **phase-down quota system**, not a product ban.

## The Actual Binding Mechanism: The HFC Phase-Down Quota

This is what genuinely governs your specification decision. The retained regulation phases down the total quantity of HFCs (CO₂-equivalent) that can be placed on the UK market:

- **2018–2020:** 63% of baseline
- **2021–2023:** 45%
- **2024–2026:** 31%
- **2027–2029:** 24%
- **2030 onward:** 21%

This drives **market availability and price** of high-GWP refrigerants (like R410A, GWP ~2088) sharply upward, effectively pushing new equipment toward lower-GWP alternatives even without a specific ban.

## Practical Implications for a 2026 Specification

1. **Avoid R410A/R404A-based chillers** — not because they're banned, but because refrigerant availability for servicing over the equipment's 15–20 year life is a real commercial and operational risk.

2. **Favour low-GWP refrigerants**, typically:
   - **R32** (GWP ~675) — mildly flammable (A2L)
   - **R1234ze** (GWP <1) — A2L, common in large chillers
   - **R290 (propane)** (GWP ~3) — A3, increasingly used in packaged units
   - **Ammonia (R717)** or **CO₂ (R744)** for certain applications

3. **A2L refrigerant safety** requires compliance with **BS EN 378** and appropriate ventilation/leak detection — factor this into plant room design.

## Divergence Warning (Verify Before Finalising)

The UK is **consulting on / revising** its F-Gas regime and may diverge from the EU's 2024 recast (EU 2024/573), which introduced stricter phase-down steps and additional bans. **Confirm the current statutory position with:**
- The **Environment Agency** (GB regulator) or **DAERA** (Northern Ireland, where the EU regulation applies under the Windsor Framework)
- The latest DEFRA guidance at time of purchase

**Northern Ireland note:** Under the Windsor Framework, NI follows the *EU* F-Gas regime, which now has different rules than GB — relevant if your portfolio spans both.

# Heat Network Pricing Under the Ofgem Regime

A few important caveats first, then the substance.

## Key caveat on timing and detail

The heat networks regulatory framework is being introduced under the **Energy Act 2023**, with Ofgem as regulator and the Heat Trust/authorisation regime being developed through consultation. As of now, **much of the detailed pricing methodology is still being finalised through secondary legislation and Ofgem consultations**. The regime is expected to be phased in from around 2025-2026 onwards. This means for a development going live in late 2026, you should treat the specifics below as directional and **verify against the latest Ofgem/DESNZ publications**, because the rules may not all be in force or fully detailed at your go-live date.

## What we can say about the pricing framework

### 1. There is no simple price cap (unlike the retail energy cap)

The government and Ofgem have signalled a preference for **consumer protection through fair pricing rules and disproportionate-price interventions**, rather than a rigid unit-price cap like the domestic gas/electricity default tariff cap. Heat networks vary enormously in cost structure (fuel source, scheme size, heat losses), so a single cap is impractical.

### 2. The "comparable to gas" / disproportionate pricing principle

The core consumer protection concept is that heat network customers should **not pay significantly more than they would on a comparable gas/electricity heating arrangement** — protecting against the "captive customer" problem (heat network customers usually cannot switch supplier).

In practice this is expected to work through:

- **Benchmarking / price comparison**: Ofgem developing reference points against which heat network prices can be assessed (e.g. what a comparable household on a conventional gas boiler would pay).
- **A "disproportionate pricing" test**: Ofgem can investigate where prices appear materially out of line with the benchmark *without adequate justification*.
- **Justification allowance**: Higher prices may be permissible where objectively justified by genuine cost factors (low-carbon heat sources, capital recovery, scheme-specific costs). The principle is not "prices must equal gas" but rather "prices must be *fair and justifiable*, and not exploit captivity."

### 3. Transparency and fair terms obligations

Regardless of price level, operators will face obligations on:
- **Price transparency** — clear tariff information, how prices are set, standing charges.
- **Fair contract terms** and billing standards.
- **Notification of price changes**.
- **Consumer complaints/redress** access (via the Energy Ombudsman and Citizens Advice).

## When Ofgem can intervene

Expected intervention triggers/powers include:

1. **Authorisation regime** — operators will need authorisation and must comply with conditions; breach is enforceable.
2. **Disproportionate pricing investigations** — where prices exceed the benchmark without justification, Ofgem can require information, investigate, and direct corrective action.
3. **Enforcement powers** — including compliance orders, potentially financial penalties, and requiring redress/compensation to consumers.
4. **Ongoing information/reporting requirements** — enabling proactive monitoring.

## Practical steps for your development

1. **Design your tariff methodology to be defensible now** — document the cost basis (capital, fuel, heat losses, O&M) so you can justify prices against a gas benchmark.
2. **Track the live consultations** from Ofgem and DESNZ, and the secondary legislation, since the precise benchmark methodology and thresholds will be defined there.
3. **Build in transparency and redress** processes from the outset (Heat Trust scheme membership is a useful proxy for good practice).
4. **Model the gas-comparison** for your specific scheme early — if you're a low-carbon scheme with higher costs, prepare the justification narrative.

# EPC Requirements in Scotland: Domestic and Non-Domestic

I should offer some important caveats before setting out the position, as this is an area where policy has shifted considerably and several proposals have been dropped or delayed.

## Domestic (the Victorian tenement flat on a PRT)

**Current minimum standard:**

There is **currently no minimum EPC rating** that a landlord must achieve to legally let a property in Scotland. This is an important distinction from England and Wales, where the Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) require a minimum EPC E for domestic lets.

Scotland consulted on introducing minimum energy efficiency standards for the private rented sector (proposals around EPC C or D by set dates), but these **regulations were not brought into force**. The previous timeline of proposed standards did not materialise as originally intended.

**What replaced/superseded this:**

The Scottish Government's approach has been folded into the wider **Heat in Buildings** agenda. The **Heat in Buildings (Scotland) Bill** was introduced (with earlier proposals around a 2028 PRS standard and 2033 for owner-occupiers), but the earlier hard targets and the "prohibition on fossil fuel heating by set dates" approach were substantially **softened and reframed** following consultation feedback. The direction of travel has moved away from fixed EPC-band deadlines toward a fabric-first / heating-systems standard.

**Practical advice for the landlord now:**
- A valid EPC is still required to market and let the property.
- There is no legal minimum band to meet at present for continued letting.
- Tenement flats carry particular challenges (solid walls, shared/common elements, conservation and listed-building constraints affecting external insulation and window replacement), so betterment works often require owners' agreement under the title deeds/tenement management scheme.

## Non-Domestic (Section 63-style regime)

**Current position:**

The existing regime is the **Assessment of Energy Performance of Non-domestic Buildings (Scotland) Regulations 2016**, made under **Section 63 of the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009**. This applies to non-domestic buildings over **1,000 m²** on sale or new lease, requiring either an **Action Plan** (identifying improvement measures) or the display of operational ratings via **Display Energy Certificates (DECs)**.

**Proposed trajectory:**

The Scottish Government has **reviewed Section 63** and signalled intention to strengthen and broaden it (potentially lowering the floor area threshold and moving toward mandatory improvement rather than deferral options). However, as with the domestic side, these proposals have been caught up in the **Heat in Buildings Bill** process and the wider reprioritisation, so firm dates and thresholds remain uncertain.

# Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 and School Procurement

## Impact on Procurement and Design Decision-Making

The Act applies to the local authority as a "public body" and fundamentally shapes how procurement decisions must be made and justified.

### The Sustainable Development Principle
The authority must demonstrate it has acted in accordance with the **sustainable development principle** – meaning decisions must balance short-term needs against the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. In practice, for a school procurement this means the authority cannot simply select lowest capital cost; it must show consideration of **whole-life value and long-term outcomes**.

### The Five Ways of Working
Decision-making must evidence:
1. **Long-term** – considering the school's whole lifecycle (design life often 60+ years), future pupil demographics, climate resilience
2. **Prevention** – e.g. designing to prevent poor educational/health outcomes, avoiding future retrofit costs
3. **Integration** – how the school supports multiple well-being goals simultaneously
4. **Collaboration** – working with other bodies (health boards, community, Welsh Government via Sustainable Communities for Learning programme)
5. **Involvement** – meaningful engagement with pupils, staff, community, diverse groups

### The Seven Well-being Goals
The procurement should contribute to goals including:
- **A Prosperous Wales** (low-carbon, resource-efficient)
- **A Resilient Wales** (biodiversity, climate adaptation)
- **A Healthier Wales** (indoor air quality, active travel, daylighting)
- **A More Equal Wales / Cohesive Communities** (community use of facilities)
- **A Wales of Vibrant Culture and Welsh Language** – note the specific duty to consider **Welsh language** provision

### Practical Procurement Mechanisms
- Setting **well-being objectives** and publishing how the project meets them
- Using **social value / community benefit clauses** in the tender (aligned with Welsh procurement policy)
- Alignment with the **Sustainable Communities for Learning** (formerly 21st Century Schools) programme funding conditions
- The **Future Generations Commissioner** can scrutinise, and there is an accountability/reporting duty
- Audit Wales assesses whether the Act's principles were applied

---

## Building Regulations Part L (2022): Wales vs England

Both nations updated Part L in 2022 as interim steps ahead of future zero-carbon standards, but **the uplifts and targets differ**.

### Wales – Part L (2022)
- Came into force **23 November 2022**.
- For **new non-domestic buildings** (which includes schools), Wales set a required **CO₂ emissions reduction of approximately 20%** against the previous 2014 baseline (Welsh Part L uplift).
- Wales retained a somewhat **different metric emphasis** and did not adopt England's Future Buildings Standard in identical form – it developed its own consultation-based standards.
- Compliance uses the **National Calculation Methodology (SBEM/DSM)** producing a Building Emission Rate (BER) that must not exceed the Target Emission Rate (TER), with additional metrics on primary energy and fabric.

### England – Part L (2021, effective June 2022)
- The **Future Buildings Standard**: new **non-domestic buildings required a ~27% reduction** in CO₂ emissions vs the 2013 baseline.
- Introduces **primary energy** as the primary performance metric plus CO₂ and fabric energy efficiency backstops.

### Key Comparative Points
| Aspect | Wales | England |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Effective date | Nov 2022 | June 2022 |
| Non-domestic CO₂ uplift | ~20% | ~27% |
| Framework | Welsh-specific standards | Future Buildings Standard |
| Devolved policy driver | Well-being Act, Net Zero Wales | Future Homes/Buildings Standard |

### EPC Requirements
- **EPCs remain required** in both nations on construction, sale or let of non-domestic buildings.
- These are **separate from Part L compliance** (which uses SBEM/SAP-based modelling at design/as-built).
- New schools should target high EPC ratings; public bodies also face **Display Energy Certificate (DEC)** obligations for occupied public buildings over 250m² showing operational energy use.

# Energy Performance Requirements: Northern Ireland Commercial Property

## EPC Requirement on Sale

**Yes, an EPC is required.** Under the **Energy Performance of Buildings (Certificates and Inspections) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2008** (as amended), an EPC must be provided whenever a building is constructed, sold, or rented.

For your office sale, the seller must:
- Make an EPC available **free of charge to prospective buyers** at the earliest opportunity
- Ensure the EPC (with its recommendation report) is provided to the person who ultimately buys the building
- Include the **asset rating (A–G)** in commercial sales particulars/advertising where produced

An EPC is valid for **10 years**. If a valid EPC already exists, a new one is not required for the sale.

## Display Energy Certificate (DEC)

**A DEC is only required if the building is occupied by a public authority and frequently visited by the public**, with a total useful floor area over **250 m²**.

For a privately owned/occupied commercial office being sold, **no DEC is required** — DECs apply to public buildings, not private commercial premises. If any part is occupied by a qualifying public body meeting the threshold, that occupier would have DEC obligations, but this is separate from the sale itself.

## How the NI Regime Differs from GB

| Feature | Northern Ireland | England & Wales | Scotland |
|---------|------------------|-----------------|----------|
| Governing law | NI 2008 Regs (as amended) | EPB (E&W) Regs 2012 | Scottish EPB Regs 2008 |
| Enforcement body | District councils | Local weights & measures / Trading Standards | Local authorities |
| MEES minimum standard | **No MEES regime** | **MEES applies** | Action Plan regime (different model) |

**Key point:** NI has **its own devolved regime** distinct from the rest of the UK. EPCs are broadly similar in appearance and methodology, but the enforcement and minimum-standards frameworks diverge significantly.

## MEES-Equivalent Restriction — The Critical Difference

**There is currently NO MEES (Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards) regime in Northern Ireland.**

In England & Wales, MEES (under the Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property) Regulations 2015) prohibits landlords from **letting** commercial property with an EPC rating below **E** (subject to exemptions), and this is tightening toward higher standards.

**However, note carefully:**
- MEES restricts **letting**, not sale — so even in E&W it would not directly prohibit a *sale*
- In **Northern Ireland, there is no equivalent letting restriction at all** — a sub-E rated property can be sold and let without a MEES-style bar

## Practical Advice for the Seller

1. **Obtain/confirm a valid EPC** before marketing — this is mandatory for the sale.
2. **No DEC needed** for a private commercial sale.
3. **No MEES restriction** currently applies to the sale or subsequent letting in NI — but flag that this may change, as NI has consulted on energy efficiency reforms.
4. A poor EPC rating won't legally block the sale in NI, but may affect **value and buyer appetite** given future-proofing concerns.
